analysis.one_liner: Cancels a 2018 rule that let insurers sell skimpy health plans exempt from Affordable Care Act protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 46 senators, died in the Senate health committee without a hearing or vote, leaving the 2018 short-term plan rule in place.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2018, the Trump administration's departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury issued a rule letting insurers sell short-term health plans for up to a year at a time, renewable for up to three years total. These plans are exempt from Affordable Care Act rules, so they can deny coverage, charge more, or exclude care for people with preexisting conditions. The No Junk Plans Act would cancel that rule and bar the agencies from issuing a similar one. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance — especially anyone with a preexisting condition — benefit, because the bill would put the 2018 rule back where it was before October 2018, restoring protections like coverage of preexisting conditions and required benefits on the individual market. It would also protect people enrolled in ACA-compliant plans from the premium increases that come when healthier customers shift into skimpy short-term plans.

how_it_helps.text: It cancels the rule that tripled the maximum length of short-term plans — from under 3 months to under 12 months, renewable up to 36 months — the plans insurers can sell without following Affordable Care Act protections.

Because short-term plans are exempt from ACA market rules, they can turn people down or charge more for preexisting conditions and skip required benefits; ending the expanded rule limits how widely those plans can be sold.
It bars the three departments from writing any substantially similar rule in the future, so the loosening could not simply be reissued.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers and brokers that sell short-term, limited-duration plans would lose a business line the 2018 rule made far larger, since the plans could no longer last up to 12 months at a time with renewals stretching to 36 months. Some buyers who preferred cheaper, skimpier coverage would lose that cheaper option and pay more for comprehensive plans.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: short-term plans are often the only affordable coverage for healthy people who earn too much for subsidies but find ACA-compliant plans expensive, and narrowing them removes a cheaper option and could push those buyers to go uninsured.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that reversing the rule does not fix the underlying affordability problem in ACA plans; it pushes some of the cost of protecting people with preexisting conditions onto healthier buyers through higher premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for the roughly millions of individual-market buyers who could otherwise be steered into plans that refuse to cover preexisting conditions, and for ACA enrollees whose premiums rise when healthy people exit. The cost falls on healthy buyers who used short-term plans as cheaper coverage, some of whom may end up uninsured rather than in a comprehensive plan. The bill is a narrow, single-purpose reversal of one regulation, so it cannot address broader affordability — but what it does target, it targets directly, and the lack of any committee action means its merits were never debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on May 21, 2019 with 46 cosponsors — 44 Democrats and 2 independents — already attached.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
The committee took no further action, and the full Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill receiving a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and brokers selling short-term, limited-duration plans, whose larger market under the 2018 rule stayed in place because the bill never moved.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, and the bill sat without action in a Republican-run committee until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The 2018 rule let these plans run for up to 12 months with renewals to 36, growing their customer base. Nullifying it would shrink that business back to its pre-2018 size.

industries.industry: Insurance brokers and agents selling short-term plans
industries.note: Brokers earn commissions selling these plans; the bill would cut off the expanded sales window the 2018 rule created.
ACA-compliant insurers would keep more healthy customers who might otherwise shift into cheaper short-term plans, helping stabilize premiums for everyone in the market.
